history_of_present_illness: Oroya fever is an acute, infectious disease, often terminating fatally, characterized by an insidious onset. The incubation period is about three weeks, with initial symptoms including malaise and apathy. This is followed by a rapidly developing anaemia of the pernicious anaemia type, accompanied by an irregular, remittent fever typically fluctuating between 100° and 102°F, though occasionally reaching 104°F. Patients experience pains in the head, joints, and bones, with tenderness particularly marked over the sternum due to bone marrow changes. A very severe anaemia develops rapidly, and delirium is often noted. Diarrhoea may occur in the later stages of the disease. In uncomplicated cases, there is no eruption.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The disease is chiefly found in towns situated in narrow, wind-protected valleys on the west side of the Andes, at elevations of 3000 to 9000 feet. Townsend suggested that a species of *Phlebotomus*, *P. verrucarum*, which is prevalent in these areas, may be the transmitting agent. Strong noted that Oroya fever was common from January to April, particularly towards the close of the warm, rainy season, with cases being rare in April and May and absent in June, July, and August. Concomitant infection with other diseases like malaria and enteric fevers, as well as verruga, is common in areas where Oroya fever prevails.
vitals: Irregular fever, remittent character, fluctuating between 100° and 102°F and only exceptionally going up to 104°F.
physical_exam: At autopsy, the skin shows the pale yellowish waxy hue typical of pernicious anaemia. Lymphatic glands are somewhat enlarged and may be oedematous. The heart is flabby, and ecchymoses may be present in the pericardium. The spleen is enlarged, shows numerous infarctions, and contains large amounts of pigment in the form of yellowish masses or granules deposited between splenic cells and in endothelial leucocytes. The liver is also enlarged, shows areas of toxic degeneration, and contains moderate amounts of pigment. The femoral marrow is soft and dark red. Microscopically, the endothelial cells of the lymphatics are noted to be distended with causative organisms. In living patients, the spleen and lymphatic glands are somewhat enlarged. Associated with profound anaemia, there may be oedema of the legs and around joints, and functional cardiac murmurs. The kidneys do not seem to be affected.
labs_and_diagnostics: The disease is caused by *Bartonella bacilliformis*. Rod-shaped organisms, 1 to 2 microns in length, are found within red cells, with infected cells containing from 1 to 30 of these elements. In sections of lymphatic glands of severe fatal cases, great numbers of these bodies are packed in endothelial cells, which then rupture, releasing the organisms. These organisms are considered intermediate between bacteria and protozoa, closely related to *Grahamella* and resembling piroplasms, especially *Theileria*. In fresh blood preparations, the rod-shaped organisms are somewhat difficult to observe but show definite gliding motility within red cells, particularly after warming. In Romanowsky-stained preparations, the 1 to 2 micron-long rods may occur singly or in numbers of 4 or 5, frequently showing V-shapes. The rods stain bluish with a deep purplish-red chromatin-stained granule at one extremity. Rounded, oval, or pear-shaped forms may also be seen. Parasites are numerous in severe cases but scarce in mild forms. There is a rapidly developing anaemia, often showing a red cell count of less than a million within a few days. Normoblasts are quite numerous, and fulminating cases show numerous megaloblasts. Polychromatophilia and poikilocytosis are noted. The red cell picture is consistent with rapidly developing pernicious anaemia, with the color index above 1. Leucocytes number about 20,000, with 60 to 70% being neutrophiles, and immature neutrophiles (metamyelocytes) are very common.
management_and_clinical_course: The disease often terminates fatally in 20 to 40% of cases within two or three weeks. As the transmitting agent is not definitely known, specific prevention measures are limited, though evidence suggests some arthropod biting at night, as disease incidence decreased when workers left affected valleys before sundown. Treatment is largely supportive nursing care. Some have reported favorable outcomes from the intravenous administration of salvarsan.
